title: How a @Scheduled method becomes a running task
summary: Registration happens in two phases: annotations are turned into Task objects as each bean is created, and nothing is actually scheduled until the context finishes refreshing.
entry: Put a breakpoint in ScheduledAnnotationBeanPostProcessor.processScheduled and start any app with @EnableScheduling. It fires once per annotated method, at startup.

steps.notice: The entire content of @EnableScheduling. One @Import, one bean definition. This is the most common shape in Spring: the annotation imports a configuration that registers a post-processor.

Runs once per bean. Note getOrder() returns LOWEST_PRECEDENCE, so by the time this sees your bean the auto-proxy creator has already wrapped it. That is why @Scheduled and @Transactional work together.
One annotation becomes one Task: CronTask, FixedDelayTask or FixedRateTask. Nothing is scheduled yet; the tasks are only collected.
Triggered by ContextRefreshedEvent. This is the phase boundary: the container is fully up before any job can fire, which is why a scheduled method never races a half-built application.
The six-step lookup, in one readable method. Follow the catch blocks rather than the happy path; the interesting outcome is the last line, a private single-thread executor nobody asked for.
Where Task objects finally reach a TaskScheduler. Everything above this line is bookkeeping.
Two lines that explain why a failing job keeps running: repeating tasks get LOG_AND_SUPPRESS, one-shot tasks get LOG_AND_PROPAGATE. Suppression keeps the schedule alive at the cost of silence.
